title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: a young ascetic visits Parvati in the forest and mocks the god she loves, and she won't stay to listen
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week of Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and Saraswati, ending with Saraswati as the speech in a giant's mouth. Where did you pause in the gap before a word? Today, the last of the five. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

A princess has left her father's palace in the Himalayas for the forest. She has tried to win the great ascetic Shiva the ordinary way: beauty, flowers, the god of love himself taking aim at Shiva. It went badly. Shiva opened his third eye and burned the god of love to ash, and walked away. So the princess changes her plan. If Shiva lives by austerity, she will out-austere him. In Kalidasa's poem, The Birth of Kumara, that's where we find her: alone, in the forest, taking up the life of an ascetic. Today, Parvati.
screen: `A PRINCESS LEAVES THE PALACE.` → `LOVE IS BURNED TO ASH.` → `SHE CHANGES HER PLAN.`

segments.voice: Kalidasa describes her austerity season by season: standing among fires in the summer heat, in cold water through winter nights, living on less and less, until she gives up eating even fallen leaves. And the poem says that's why those who know the old stories call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf. Then one day a visitor comes: a young ascetic with matted hair, polite, admiring. He asks why someone so lovely is doing all this. And when he learns it's for Shiva, he starts, very gently, to make fun of her choice. Shiva? The one who wears snakes and ash? Who rides an old bull and haunts cremation grounds? Nobody even knows who his family is. A princess like you, with him? Parvati doesn't laugh along, and she doesn't crumble. She defends Shiva, point by point, and then she does something sharper. She tells her companion to stop him, because the one who speaks badly of a great soul does wrong, and so does the one who stays and listens. And she turns to walk away. That's when the young ascetic drops the disguise. He was Shiva all along, testing her. And in the poem, he says that from now on, he's hers, won by her austerity. So here is Parvati as a character. Not a girl waiting to be chosen. She is the one who chooses, and then outlasts the god of austerity at his own practice, and finally won't even stand still while he's insulted to her face. Even when it's him doing the insulting.
screen: `AUSTERITY, SEASON BY SEASON.` · `APARNA: NOT EVEN A LEAF.` · `A VISITOR MOCKS HER CHOICE.` · `SHE TURNS TO WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `IT WAS SHIVA ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: stand by what you love. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone or something you're devoted to that others don't quite understand: a person, a calling, a place, a practice. Hear, for a moment, the gentle mocking voice: really, that? Then notice what in you answers. Not with anger. Just steady. Let the steadiness sit in the body, in the spine, in the breath. If you pray, you can bring that devotion before Parvati or before God. If you don't, just stay steady. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name over these five; and some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods: the patient one in the forest, the warrior on the lion. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, when someone makes light of something you love, try answering once, steadily, without a fight. Tomorrow, Parvati and an empty kitchen. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Parvati's austerity to win Shiva is remembered in festivals such as Hartalika Teej, when some Hindu women fast and pray in her honor, and her story is told in the Puranas and in Kalidasa's poem.

original.note: Sanskrit: Aparna. Kalidasa says those who know the old stories call Parvati this because she gave up even fallen leaves.

trapdoor: what you thought: Parvati is the gentle wife, waiting at Shiva's side.
what it means: she chooses Shiva, outlasts him at austerity, and won't stay to hear him mocked.
what a scholar hears: Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, canto five: the Aparna verse, the brahmacharin's mockery, and Shiva's self-revelation.
recall: the year just walked and kept

notes: Kumarasambhava canto 5 paraphrased (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm: the five-fires summer austerity and winter water, giving up fallen leaves (5.28, Aparna), the brahmacharin's mockery (snakes, ash, bull, cremation ground, unknown lineage), her rebuke that the listener also incurs sin, her turning to leave, and Shiva's words that he is now her servant 'bought by austerity'. The title 'The Birth of Kumara' is a translation of the poem's name.
The burning of Kama is in canto 3; Shiva Purana tells the same arc. Day 679 described Parvati as Brahmacharini briefly; this day tells the poem's scene.
'Some Hindus hear Parvati and Durga as one Goddess in two moods' is attributed; confirm.
howItsDone: Hartalika Teej is associated with Parvati's austerity; 'some Hindu women' avoids a count. Confirm.
Original: अपर्णा. The meaning comes from the poem's own explanation.
Editor pass: in canto 3 Kama aims at Shiva at the gods' bidding, so 'on her behalf' became 'taking aim at Shiva'; cut the unsupported 'doing what nobody expected'.
